projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Dale Wolf was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So what we're going to do is you're just going to tell me a little story.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Tell me your full name, your date, when you were born, where you were born, who your parents were, what they did, and then we'll go from there. Go ahead any time you want to start.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: I'm Dale Edward Wolf and I was born on a farm in Kearney, Nebraska. My folks were Harry and Irene --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Videographer
sp.p: Sorry to interrupt.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Look at me.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Sorry. Start over again, shall we?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Go ahead?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: I'm Dale Edward Wolf, and I was born in Kearney, Nebraska on a farm about eight miles from the city of Kearney. And my parents were Harry and Irene Wolf, and they were farmers at a time when farming was a very tough business.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. Did you go to school through there or did you go to --

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Yes, I went to a one-room country school where in the first eight grades -- which is about a mile from my house, in the first eight grades, there were 12 kids in school. Very small, as you could tell. And I was there, I skipped two grades during the first eight grades, so I was only there six years. But it's kind of a fun time when we walked across one mile to school, and one mile back, of course. And it was a great way to grow up.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Do you have any other siblings?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Yes, I have four sisters, so you can see I was spoiled by my mother and all those four girls.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And where did you fit?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: I was the second oldest.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. Now where did you go to high school?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: I went to high school in Kearney, Nebraska, and it was the time I graduated from there in 1940. And as I said, eight miles from where I grew up, so about when I became a junior, I began to drive to school, and take my sister with me and several neighbor kids.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, December 7, 1941 -- now, when you were in high school, you graduated in '40. Right?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Were you on to college after that?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Yes. And it's an interesting story, at least for me, because I was so poor at the time, and the farm was so poor, that I had no idea that I could go to college. And exactly two days before college started at the University of Nebraska, my uncle came out from Kearney and said, What are you going to do? I hadn't even thought about that because there really wasn't an opportunity to go anyway. And he said, Look, you're going to go to college, and I'll loan you 200 dollars, and I want you to get on down there. So two days later, I went. And so I went to the University of Nebraska, and I was 15 at the time. I went to school for a few weeks before I became 16. But it was one of the best things, and I think back about how close it became that I might not have gone at all.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So when you were there at -- when you were there at college in Nebraska, that's when World War II would have started, right?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Yes, mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Do you remember that Sunday?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Oh, yes, I certainly do. I should say.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Tell me about that Sunday.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Well, you know, it was a big time. December 7, 1941, was a time when I think everybody remembers where they were. I was in school, in class at the time I heard this. And it obviously changed the world forever, and certainly changed my life forever.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What impact did it have on you at the time?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Well, I was in ROTC at Nebraska, at the University of Nebraska, and obviously, coming from a farm, I had the choice of either staying in ROTC or getting deferred, because I was on the farm and producing food. And I remember the decision-making process at the time, and the people I talked to. And I got excellent advice, which was said, Get on in there and do your thing. So sometime later, of course, the whole group was called in to the Army.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did you -- were you able to graduate --

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- first?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: I had gone in in April 1943, so I had been there almost three years, not quite, but I had enough credit so that when I went back for six weeks later, while being in the Army, they considered that I had enough credits to graduate. So it was when I was in the Army that I learned that I had gotten my degree.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, I know, like my dad did here, my dad and the whole gang of them were down at the University of Delaware, ROTC, and they were actually -- they graduated probably a couple years before you did, because before Pearl Harbor, there were already up at Camp Upton in New York, 198th Coast Artillery.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did you have a similar group that you were involved in with the ROTC? Did you go to the Nebraska National Guard, or how did that -- tell me how that worked.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: I was called into basic training at Camp Roberts, California. The whole group was called into there. I was in a field artillery section of the ROTC. Then from there, we went to Fort Sill, Oklahoma, for Officer's Training School. And then graduating from there, I went to Camp Roberts. Let's see, where did I go next? Camp Van Dorn, Mississippi. And from there, I was sent overseas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. So you were in -- and you went in -- you went in college, your freshman year would have been 1940. So you would have been a sophomore in 1941. Right?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So you were able to go the whole to '43, did you say?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Yes, till April of '43.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: When you graduated?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: I didn't graduate. I actually didn't get a degree until 1945.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: But in April of '43, they activated the ROTC unit.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. Okay. So then you went to those various things. Where was your last -- and then did you go overseas -- tell me -- bring me up to where you were doing your training?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And then when you went into the real -- I mean, when you got involved with the real service?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Yes, well, during Basic Training, and then I was fortunate to be able to go to Officer's Training School, and that was a good place to get a lot of good training, and then I was called to Camp Van Dorn, Mississippi, for a while. Then I was selected to go overseas, I say selected, and went to Fort Lewis, Washington, where we caught a ship to Hawaii, and then a ship to Okinawa. And I went to Okinawa on April 4, 1945, which was four days after the invasion of Okinawa.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Then what did you do there? Tell me a little bit about that.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: I was a forward observer with the infantry, and that was my training. That's what I had done. And when I arrived in Okinawa -- I was with the 306th Field Artillery Battalion. And when I arrived there, every single officer had been killed in the first four days. So I recall the moment when I picked up the map and the gun of the previous forward observer. And I think it took about two days to get to the front lines. And there I was on the front lines in Okinawa without knowing much about what was going on.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How long were you there?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: I was there until the end of the war, and then we went to Cebu City, so I was there roughly 95 days. And then the whole unit was moved to Cebu City in the Philippines to be trained for the invasion of Japan.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And just continue. Tell me what --

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Well, Okinawa, to me, was a -- I was the youngest of any of the group that I was around. I was with the 77th Infantry Division, as a forward observer. You may remember that Okinawa, which is 60 years ago, it rained all the time during April and March and -- April, May, June, and it just seemed to rain all the time. I've never been so wet in my life. And it was a very, very tough battle, as you know. Probably the most people were killed in Okinawa of any battle in history at that time. Almost 250,000 Japanese and Okinawans were killed, 13,000 Americans were killed. So it was a difficult time. But I was the youngest person in my group. As a forward observer, you're sitting on the front lines with three other people, sometimes four. And it's supposed to be rotated. The officers rotated, the staff is rotated. But since I was the only officer, there wasn't an opportunity to be rotated. So my staff would be rotated, but I was not. So I sat in the mud for a whole long time, and it was a tough battle. And there was a time when we moved very, very slowly in Okinawa. You might move 20 feet a day, or you might move 20 feet in three days. There was just -- I remember one young gentleman came up to the front lines, and said, Well, where are the front lines? And I said, They're right there, they're right just two feet away. But it was the time when the Japanese were stuck in caves on Okinawa, and it was a very difficult time getting them out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did you call in also the support in the harbor?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: No?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: No. We called in the support -- well, we could use the support from the harbor, but -- because it would be transferred over, but my direct connection was with the artillery, which was back, of course, quite a ways from the front line. And I recall one day, when we were pinned down, we just couldn't see where the fire was coming from. And so I had to get out of -- I either, had a choice of selecting one of my men to go someplace to find out how to do this, or do it myself. And I've always said that I really didn't have the guts, really, to select someone to go do that, so I did it myself. And for that, I got a Bronze Star. But it was mostly because I really didn't have the courage to select one of those people to go out and try to get -- find out what was going on. But it was a very successful move because I moved through the open field and came back and selected the right fire at the right place to solve the problem. And someone said, Well, why did you get an award for that? And I've told my kids, you know, getting awards is mostly about having someone write it up. It so happened that one of the staff sergeants in my group was good enough to write it up. But there are a whole lot of people in wars that do a lot of wonderful things that you never hear about because there isn't someone to write it up.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So how long were you on -- how long did that battle go on that you were involved with?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: About 90 days. And then, as I say, when the atomic bomb was dropped later, then, of course, the end of the war. But we were in the Philippines, our whole unit, 77th Infantry Division, training for the invasion of Japan at the time. And I had been injured on Okinawa, so I wasn't in very good physical shape. But we moved to Hokkaido, Japan as a group, to secure the island, if you will, secure the country. And I was there just a couple of weeks when I was sent back to Galesburg, Illinois, in the hospital. So I spent nine months in the hospital in Galesburg, Illinois. And it was a time when -- I certainly remember a whole lot about that, but I think back at the time, when we went into Japan as a group that was supposed to keep it secure, and the people were all so kind, and it was really a time when I grew up a whole lot, by being in the Army. I wouldn't do it again, but it was a time when it certainly matured me.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did -- how were you hurt?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: I was blown out of a shell hole. And at the same time -- on the front lines, because a big shell landed right next to us and killed one of my men, but all I was done was blown out. And later, I had a great problem with a disk, two disks were herniated, and caused a big problem, and that's why I spent so much time in the hospital later on.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So did you get a Purple Heart?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: I got a Purple Heart, I did, indeed.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Was that friendly fire or --

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Oh, no. I wish. No, it wasn't friendly at all. There was a whole lot of fire going on at that time. The Japanese had some awfully skilled people, and a lot of our best generals in Okinawa. And their idea wasn't to win the war. Their idea, as you perhaps have read some of the books, was really to kill as many Americans as they could. And that was their goal. And so they sent fire of all kinds. And it was well-organized because a lot of these times, the equipment would be in a cave, and they would roll it out and fire it, then roll it back in on tracks. Many of the caves I saw where they had tracks, they would roll the equipment in and out. So it was very difficult to spot, very difficult to control.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Why Okinawa? Why did they pick Okinawa for that? What was the -- I mean, I know, like, Iwo Jima, there was a reason for that, because of the air field there, and the bombers being able to get back or some safe place to land if they had an emergency. What was the big deal with Okinawa?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Well, the Americans, we chose Okinawa. "We" is a very large word. We chose Okinawa because it was the last big fortification before the invasion of Japan. And there was no way that the Americans were going to have that not secure when they invaded Japan. This was supposed to be the last battle before the invasion of Japan. And it was, of course, until the atomic bomb was dropped. But this was -- the idea was that we must be able to park our equipment there, we must be able to have the ships close by. And we can't be bothered by fire from Okinawa while we're trying to get into Japan.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How did you finally clean them all out of there?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Well, it was one minute at a time, really. It was very, very difficult. And very sad, really, far too many people killed. Think of the number of people, a quarter of a million people killed on Okinawa. It's unbelievable today to think of those kinds of numbers. And a lot of Okinawans, a lot of Japanese, and of course, far too many Americans were killed, and were wounded, one way or the other. But it was just -- you know, it's a very small island, very difficult to move, the terrain was awful, the weather was awful, and they were just prepared for us. They dug in and they were not about to be conquered by anybody.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did -- as the battle, as the days went on, did they have a lot of air power, or was -- their air power was pretty much shut down by then, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Oh, no.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: No?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: You remember that during Okinawa was the time when they had hundreds of kamikaze planes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Kamikazes in the harbor, yes, I remember.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: And that was the greatest concentration of kamikaze of any time during the war. And I think the Navy lost far more people than they thought they would lose. They sunk a number of ships. They killed a number of people. So it was a very difficult time for those in the Navy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, how about where you were, though? Was there a lot of fire power going on from Japanese airplanes, or --

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Not so much from airplanes because they had bigger targets. I mean, they were targeting the ships.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: But there was a whole lot of small fire and a whole lot of artillery, and things like that, that came from the cave areas and other parts of the island. But mostly, the air power, I think, was pretty well limited to the ships.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How about our air power? Were they able to back you guys up, or --

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Not very well, because of the very small hunk of geography and very difficult to find a particular cave that you're trying to knock out, a particular piece of artillery. So the air power, although it was good probably in strafing somewhere far back, it was not very effective for those of us on the front line because it was difficult to get them to the right place at the right time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Do you remember the last day you were there or the last big battle there? I mean, the --

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: I surely do. I surely do. There was Sugar Loaf Hill and Shuri, which has gotten so much publicity. But I just remember practically every day I was there, I remember, because of the things that happened, and the difficult time -- it surprised me, as I say, I was -- all the folks around me were considerably older, a lot of them were from Philadelphia, by the way, in the 77th Infantry Division. And here's a young kid from the farm in Nebraska trying to figure out what to do with the artillery in the front lines in Okinawa. I must confess, I was way over my head. But we had a great group of people fighting on our side. But the thing that surprised me is how difficult -- you think you go into a war and you're going to do all these wonderful things at that battle and you're going to win quickly. It just didn't happen, because we couldn't move the Japanese back because they were secured so well. And I think that, to answer your question, there wasn't a specific battle that was the final, we finally covered the island, but it was just one Japanese at a time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: I mean, did you get a phone call that said, You got it all cleaned up, we're ready to rock and roll out of here?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: It just was --

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: It was not that. It wasn't dramatic. I remember, though, one thing that happened that I thought was so fascinating to me. One day, we awakened from the foxhole, and it had stopped raining. And all of a sudden, for a period of probably three hours, there wasn't a shot fired on either side. I think both sides had decided that they were going to take the morning off. And I still remember that day because the Japanese were getting out of their foxholes drenched as we were, but there wasn't a shot fired until about 11:00 in the morning. Then all of a sudden, the war began again. You say, How can that happen? But it did. And I think one of the funny things at the time, my now-wife Clarice, was my girlfriend, and she sent a little tape over that she had done a song. And so I had gotten some mail about once every three weeks or something, you'd get some mail on the front lines. But here's this tape, and I'm figuring out how am I going to play this thing in a foxhole? So we've talked about that over the years.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did you ever hear the song?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Oh, yes. Much later, I might say. Much later.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So you went -- so then you went there to Japan, and you were sent back. Did you go through -- going over, you left out of Washington?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Right?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Fort Lewis, Washington.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Troop ship?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Went to Hawaii.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Troop ship?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And went over to Hawaii, troop ship?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: And then went over, troop ship, over to Okinawa itself.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How did they ship you back when you were injured?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: I came back, I went to a hospital ship in Yokohama, Japan, from Hokkaido, where I was stationed, and from there, by air, a hospital plane, to San Francisco and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So you were actually hit on Okinawa?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. All right. Then you had a hospital ship back to San Francisco?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Yes. Well, a hospital plane.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Plane?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: From a hospital ship in Yokohama, Japan, and then from there, a number of us were evacuated on a hospital plane to San Francisco, and then Omaha, Nebraska, and then Galesburg, Illinois.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So they didn't keep you at the Presidio, at the hospital there?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: No, we never went there. We went kind of a direct flight. Fortunately, we were weathered-in in Omaha, Nebraska, on the way to Galesburg, Illinois, so I could call Clarice and say, I'm home. She said, What are you doing home so soon? You're supposed to come home later. This is November of 1945. And so it was a time I remember very well. I was fortunate, indeed.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So now, you get back in the hospital, then tell me a little bit about your years from there to here, to now.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: I went in in November '45, and I decided that -- they kept wanting to operate on my back, and I just didn't want them to be operating on my back, so we thought we could cure it some other way, so with a whole lot of bedrest and a whole lot of other things. But finally, in June of '46, I decided I really just had to get out of there, so I asked to get out of there. They asked me to stay in the Army on a permanent basis. I chose not to. I figured I was playing poker all night, bridge all day in the hospital, and just, if I would have stayed there, I would have been a complete bum. So I went back -- I was married December 31st, 1945, and while I was in the hospital, and decided that -- Clarice and I decided we just had to go do something different. So I went back to the University of Nebraska, where I had graduated, and said, Okay, what do I do now? I didn't have a plan. And they said, Why don't you go to graduate school? Picked up the phone, talked to a professor at Rutgers University in New Jersey, and the guy offered me a job immediately to go to graduate school and get a Ph.D. at Rutgers. And so that's what we did. In June of -- the same month, we came to New Brunswick, New Jersey, where I studied for a Ph.D. in agriculture. And I was fortunate at the time to study a science that was brand new at the time, how to control weeds with chemicals. So I have the great distinction of having the first Ph.D. in weed science in the United States. And that and a nickel won't get you much. But it was an interesting time for us. It was a field that was new. And later, when I graduated in 1950 -- '49, the DuPont Company was interested in expanding into that area. And so I was interviewed a number of times, and offered a job in research in DuPont in Wilmington. And we chose to do that. So on January -- about the middle of January, 1950, Clarice and I came to Wilmington, Delaware, for the first time. And it's been all great since then. And I've said that timing in life is a whole lot more important than other things, because I think when I was there, it was at the right time, and I was fortunate, indeed. And DuPont was expanding into agriculture at the time, and I had been fortunate enough to write a book on weed science while I was getting my advanced degree with two other professors; and so it was, there again, something that had created a little bit of buzz at the time. And so the company thought I could help them get into this new science. And then about four years later, they thought I would be a good salesman in California, so we moved to California. And so over the years, I think I had 19 different jobs in DuPont, and fun jobs, really, all of them. I became chairman of the board of the pharmaceutical business and head of the agriculture business, both growing, exciting businesses, and worldwide business, particularly in the agricultural area. So I had a chance to travel to Japan. When I left DuPont in '87, 62 percent of our business in agriculture was outside the U.S. So I spent a lot of time in Japan and France and Germany and the UK and Australia, and it was a wonderful way to see the world again. On my last trip with DuPont into the Far East, I went back to Okinawa, by the way, with Clarice, to see some of the those little old hills I had been crawling over years before. So it was a very interesting time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So then the politicians got ahold of you in '87?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Yes. Mike Castle and I had been on a number of committees together, he always representing government and I always representing the private sector, whether it was in child care or agriculture or environment. And so one day, I got a call from Mike Castle, and he said, Let's have breakfast, Dale. I thought, Uh-oh, another volunteer job. Man. So then Mike said, Look, I need you to run economic development for the State of Delaware, and I'd like to have you do it as soon as you can. Well, I had just brought in a new vice president into the ag business, Jack Kroll, who had just been there a short while, and I said, Well -- I talked to the bosses at DuPont, and because I was kind of interested, I knew probably more people in Tokyo than I knew in Delaware at the time, and it was interesting. But Clarice and I had decided we wanted to stay in Delaware the rest of our lives, and this would be a good thing to do. So I talked to the boss, and they said, Well, if you'll wait a while, then I will go. This is in November, I think, when Mike called me. So I then left in May. And Mike said, Okay, I'll wait. And that surprised me. So then I became the director of development for the State of Delaware, which was I think one of the most fun jobs, and a good way to enter state government here, because you had housing for the poor at that time, you had tourism, you had economic development, and you had the capital budget. So it was a great way to get to know a whole lot of people in a hurry. And then the rest, perhaps, is history. But a year later, there was an opening to run for lieutenant governor, and as you know, they're elected separately here, but Mike convinced me to run for that office; and fortunately, I won. And then the best part, of course, is that Mike was good enough to get elected to Congress four years after that, so I could become governor a short while. Now, could I have planned that? Of course, you can't, but there again, just all the incidentals of being in the right place at the right time, and being willing to take chances.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: It is amazing if you look back on the story you just told me, it was timing.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Oh, all of it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Timing. Even when you started, when you were talking about going to college. Here, you're waiting around, it's two weeks to start, and all of a sudden, your uncle showed up.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You're right. And it is, life is.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: And I tell my children and my grandchildren, particularly, you've got to plan ahead as to what you want to do. I must say, I was one of the worst planners I've ever seen, but there again, when I first went to the University of Nebraska with that 200 dollars, I had four jobs when I was a freshman there. I scooped pig manure, I counted seeds, I waited tables, and, you know, it all worked, but it all worked because I was there and you could do that stuff at that time. And I think it's so critical that you just take advantage of the opportunities that come along.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Absolutely.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Fortunately, I've been able to do that. But -- and I've loved, I must say, I have talked to a lot of people who don't like their jobs, don't like what they're doing, but I loved every job I had, and I think it's important to like what you do. I liked the people that I worked with. And I worked with some great people.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: The way you reminded me a lot of my dad was way long ago, when I first had met you and stuff, that's the way my dad was. My dad always was happy to be around people.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You've always been happy to be around people.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And I used to think, God, does that man ever get mad at anything? Your kids would probably tell me different. But it's like enjoying, enjoying life, enjoying what you're doing.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Oh, sure. And enjoying the people around you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Absolutely.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: And really, being willing to listen to good advice. And I've gotten a lot of good advice over the years.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Let's go back to, if -- would you go in again, like you went in before? I mean, in the military.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: You bet. Absolutely. Absolutely. Here's a little kid from a farm, never been -- I'd never been out of Nebraska. One time, actually, when I got a scholarship with the 4-H Club and went to Chicago one weekend for some meeting, but that's the only time I'd ever been out of Nebraska. And first thing, you know, the opportunities the Army opened up for me, the people I met, the people with whom I worked over those many years, and the training I received. And probably the most important training is how to work with people. And certainly, you have to do that. And the Army did a great job of that. I wouldn't go in again if I knew I was going to have all those battles and have people around me killed on Okinawa, so many, many people. A dozen people were killed who were no further than two feet from me. And you say, how did that happen? Well, that's the way it is. And some people are more fortunate than others. And I know how fortunate I was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. Then tell me, then, your generation, which has been called the greatest generation, tell me a little bit about that. I mean, why do you think -- not why do you think that.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: That phrase. Tell me about that phrase. Why do you think your generation has been called the greatest generation?

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Well, for one thing, I believe that, you know, we all were dedicated to do a good job at what we were doing. Not that they aren't today, but there weren't the questions around about, why are you doing it? Even going into the Army, as I said, I remember the very distinct decision I had to make, because I could have been deferred. I could have been deferred because I was on the farm. And I remember the discussions I had with the professors, with my family, about do you do it or don't you do it? And I just -- I decided that, with a lot of advice from folks, that, really, one doesn't really have a choice in that you really need to go do what you need to do. And there were a whole lot of times, TJ, when I would rather have not done it, later, but there was a time I didn't really think there was another choice. I had a job to do, and everybody else was doing their job, and I should be a part of that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What -- give me some comments you would pass on to this generation, or future generations.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Well, I'm not one to give advice, but having four children and 13 grandchildren and two great-grandchildren, I think they're all so much more well-educated than I was at the time, at the same age. They have seen so many things happen around them that I didn't see. And I think we're okay just the way we are. I think the people -- my family, of course, like anything, that we loved the kids and are very close to them, and they're going to do just fine the way they are. And I don't think they need much advice from us, because they can give us some advice on what to do these days. But we were at a time when there was a great consensus in the country as to what to do, and that makes it easier. I think there wasn't -- there weren't many people you talked to on the street who said, Don't you dare go do that. We shouldn't be in this war anyway. I think there was a consensus that this is what we have to do if we're going to be safe. And we did.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Pascal? PASCAL: For our generation, and when we hear about the conflict, we currently have, with 1800 dead people over a period of two years or something, when you were approached back then as a farm boy on a ship, on a fleet, going toward Okinawa, knowing this would be like a crucial, huge battle, the likelihood of you personally getting killed may be 50 percent --

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Or more.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- how was -- explain the fear and the feeling that goes for a young man, going into this situation. But as you answer, please look at TJ.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Several weeks ago, I discovered a letter that I had written my sister the day before I went to the front lines, and telling her of the fear, and might not see her again. And so you bet. A whole lot of fear at the time. And I said, Don't you dare tell my folks, don't tell my Clarice how scared I was.

sp.speaker: Pascal
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now that you've got the man all upset --

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Pascal
sp.p: I apologize for that.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: No. That's good.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: That was a good one.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: That's good.

sp.speaker: TJ
sp.p: We'll just --

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: You have more than enough. Cut all the bad parts out.

sp.speaker: TJ
sp.p: Your role, as far as Delaware goes, being lieutenant governor, being in economic development, being eventually governor, and I know, probably, that you read and studied about Delaware's involvement during World War II, which we had a hell of an involvement, this little state did.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And I think it's the little state that could. I mean, all these people are trying to come up with all these phrases of we're the best or you're the rest or whatever.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: But we're like the little state that could. I mean, we had damn near three-quarters of the population was involved in the war effort here.

sp.speaker: Dale Wolf
sp.p: Yeah, and that's so small, you could figure out how many were involved because it's small enough where you were each close to each other. In Nebraska, 200-some miles from one coast to another, from one end to the other, they weren't sure what was going on with the rest of the folks. But you are. You could be here. And I think Delaware is, to me, one of the best states. That's why Clarice and I decided to stay here the rest of our life, because it is a wonderful place to be. I mean, Delaware is a small state, and being a tiny bit in government and politics has been awfully important to us, to just to be a part of the system. But there are a lot of great things happening in Delaware. People know each other, people work together. People find a way to do something. As you say, a state that can make something happen. I always remember a wonderful little story from a 13-year-old girl who had moved from Delaware to Pennsylvania, and I had had her, while I was president of the Senate, had her sit on my chair and be there. And she said, you know, I've been here six months, and I haven't met the governor yet. And I thought, that says a lot about Delaware, because the kids all know who -- you can go to a dinner party here and you know both senators and representatives and governor and lieutenant governor will all be there. You can't do that in other states. Yes, you can do it once every ten years, but I think it's a wonderful opportunity to grow up in a state like Delaware and to be a part of it.
